pages.text:
Goldman Sachs Interview Experience 
 
Ahaan Desai - TY CE 
Eligibility Criteria  
CS/IT: 7+ CGPA 
EXTC/Electronics: 8+ CGPA 
 
Application and Pre Placement Talk 
On 27th July, we received an email from the TPO, informing us about the 
Goldman Sachs Campus Drive. GS took the PPT on 1st July at 5 pm, where 
they spoke about what their company does, their values etc. I’d suggest 
taking notes of the PPT as it might come up in interviews. 
 
Online Assessment​
1st July 
The OA was conducted on hackerrank on the same day as PPT, between 7-8 
pm. 170 students gave the OA. 
There were 3 programming questions, 10 MCQs and 1 HR question. 
Tab switching was not allowed. Video was not monitored. 
 
a) Programming Questions 
i) Given a range (l, r) [l & r not included] , find pairs (x,y) in this range such 
that: 
   sum of perfect divisors of x = y + 1 
   sum of perfect divisors of y = x + 1 
   x != y

[Perfect divisors of a number include all divisors except the number itself.] 
 For example, if x = 140 and y = 195, the sum of perfect divisors of x is 196 = 
195+1 and that of y is 141 = 140 + 1. Constraints: r <= 50,000. 
ii) A problem that involved finding aliases for a particular name 
For example if original names = ["ABC", "DEF", "GHI"] and alias = ["AXY", 
"DJK", GPS"] then ABC -> AXY, DEF -> DJK , GHI -> GPS. 
Basically, the aliases should be mapped such that the first characters of 
original and alias names should be the same.  
 
iii) You were given station data for 3 weather stations for N days. Station 1 
had all the data of N days perfectly, while station 2 and 3 had some missing 
and repeated days. The task was to find the minimum number of columns to 
delete such that the data is consistent. Consistency in this case meant that 
all 3 stations should have the same set of days (even with same counts). 
The test case below will make this question clear. 
Station 1: 1 5 7 6 4 3 2​
Station 2: 5 3 3 2 2 1 4 
Station 3: 3 5 4 4 4 1 6 
In this case, a possible case would be to delete columns 3,4,5,7, resulting in 
1 5 3 
5 3 1 
3 5 1 
So the columns to delete are 4. We had to find the minimum possible 
number of columns to delete  
 
b) MCQs 
10 MCQs were asked on mathematics, DSA topics and Java OOPS . These 
were easy to medium problems, DSA was just theoretical stuff. I don't 
remember the exact questions but the rough topics are below 
Math: Equation solving, finding area of an irregular shape

Java OOPS: Stuff about object creation and inheritance  
DSA: A question on simulation using stack and heap, types of self balancing 
trees. 
c) HR question 
A single HR question was there for which a response had to be typed. The 
question was: "What will you do if your classmate can't work on a project 
anymore?” 
 
My Experience:  
I started with the DSA questions first. I solved two questions out of three, 
and both in Python.  
 
Q1 solution: 
The bruteforce for this question (generating all pairs and checking the 
condition) would take O(r^2 sqrt(r)) time complexity. There are r^2 pairs in 
the worst case and time to calculate perfect divisor sum takes sqrt(r) time 
(assuming optimal algorithm which just checks till sqrt(n))]. Since r was <= 5 
* 10^4 , it would take ~6 x 10^11 operations which is not feasible. (feasible 
should mean <= 10^8). 
 
My approach (while not the most optimal one) had time complexity r*sqrt(r) 
: ~10^7 operations, which worked. 
I iterated over the range (x=l+1, x<=r-1; x++) [or range(l+1, r) in python] and 
for each number x in the range, I calculated the sum of perfect divisors (s). 
Hence a possible y for this x is s - 1, as per the given condition. 
Now I calculated the sum of the perfect divisors of this y , and checked if it is 
equal to x+1. 
If it is, then (x,y) is a valid pair. 
(I've left out some key edge cases here - see if you can identify them. These 
edge cases were the reason it took me so long to solve this problem.)

An optimisation would be to precompute divisor sums up to N = 50,000 , 
which would take NlogN time, and then a y for an x can be found and 
checked in constant time. But it was not needed for the problem. 
 
Q2 solution:  
A use of a hashmap would easily solve this problem. Each first character 
should be mapped to the alias, and each real name should be mapped to its 
first character.  
Suppose there is AXY (alias) and ABC (real), and map1 stores character to 
alias mappings, and map2 stores mappings from real name to first character.  
We could do something like map1[map2[“ABC”]] = map1[“A”] = AXY. 
There was some existing code, to which we had to tailor our solution and 
return values. 
 
Q3 
Nobody who gave the OA solved this question (at least to my current 
knowledge). The solution might have involved dynamic programming 
(especially computing longest common subsequences) and use of sets to 
filter out invalid days.  
(Solution left as exercise to reader - contact me if you solve it) 
 
OA Results: 
19 students were selected from the OA.

Interviews 
19th July 
Out of the 19 selected from the OA, 2 people got selected elsewhere. They 
called one more person on the day of the interviews. So a total of 18 
candidates gave interviews.  
 
As the hiring team had to catch a flight in the afternoon, all candidates were 
called at 7 am in the morning. At around 8 am, the hiring team were all at 
campus, and they introduced themselves and asked if we had any doubts. 
Then they started the interviews shortly after. 4 people from Goldman Sachs 
were present to conduct the entire hiring process, plus TPO faculty and 
student representatives. The interview was conducted at the VJTI racing 
office and the EV lab, as the main TPO office was under renovation.  
 
The team took 3 rounds of hiring, with shortlisting after every round.  
The first two rounds were: 
1.​ DSA + Resume projects 
2.​ A high level description/design of an application.  
 
Some people gave the DSA round first and then the design round, while 
others had the design round first. Some people only gave the DSA round. But 
whoever gave the design round also gave the DSA round.  
 
I had the DSA round first and then the design round.

Round 1 
8:30 am 
Duration: 30 mins 
 
I was the second person to give the first round. I went into the interview 
cabin, greeted my interviewer and got seated. Without further ado, I gave 
my introduction. She read my resume and started asking questions on my 
first listed project. 
 
Q1. Describe the high level architecture of your application, mention what 
technologies that you have used for each part of the application, and how 
they communicate within each other. 
Now this was a recipe app I’d made as part of the Inheritance mentorship 
program. The app frontend was made using flutter, and had 3 backend 
servers, one for the main data (recipe data, user data etc.), one for gathering 
ingredient prices from various grocery websites and a machine learning 
model for recipe recommendation. Click here to know more about the 
project. 
So I described the architecture on paper and told her how data is being 
displayed/transferred. She asked how the frontend gets data from the 
backend so I mentioned that the data from the backend is being exposed via 
a REST API. Then she asked me if I modeled the application in a sort of 
microservices type architecture to which I said that I was going in that 
direction but it wasn't a traditional microservice architecture. 
 
Q2. What databases have you used for the application, and where have you 
gotten the data? 
I mentioned that I used MongoDB, as at the time of building the project that 
was the only database I was familiar with. I’d also listed a project using SQL

in my project, so she asked a bunch of follow-ups related to the tradeoffs of 
MongoDB and SQL. 
​
1. Why did you choose MongoDB over SQL? 
Reason listed above, I did not know SQL much back then, and I mentioned 
that I only got well versed with it after studying DBMS in college.  
 
2. Would you migrate the database to use SQL?  
Now there was a lot of discussion here. Initially, I said I would migrate, as the 
data in my project was structured only and there was no special reason to 
use MongoDB instead. Then she asked me the differences between 
MongoDB vs SQL, is SQL more efficient than MongoDB, further questioning 
on why I would switch to SQL. I highlighted the main differences between 
them, for the efficiency part I really didn't say much, rambled a bit about 
joins in SQL, and that joins don't exist in MongoDB (and spoke about the 
equivalent). I mentioned that my main reason for SQL preference now is that 
queries in SQL are easier to write, as opposed to mongodb. In mongodb, 
querying is a bit tedious, json objects are used in queries, where nesting can 
get a bit deep and hard to understand.  
 
3. Where did I get the data?​
I got the data from a publicly available dataset on Kaggle. My interviewer 
was not aware about Kaggle so I gave her a brief explanation about what 
Kaggle is and why it's used by developers.  
 
Q3. How will you implement the addition of new recipes? 
Well this question started off with “is there any intercommunication 
between servers?”. There was no intercommunication between the servers 
as they were mostly standalone. But my ML model was trained on recipe 
data and I was using the same data as my database. Now my app also

doesn't support adding new recipes as of now, so she followed up with “How 
will you add the functionality of adding new recipes?”. This part was pretty 
straightforward, I said I'd implement a form in the frontend, and I’d send the 
form to my backend server, and also my ML server as its being trained on the  
recipe data itself. In the ML server I was storing vector embeddings of recipe 
data, so the model could directly use those embeddings to evaluate similar 
recipes. So the recipe would need to be sent to the ML model too. I 
mentioned the flow would be  
1.​ An API call to the backend server 
2.​ An API call to the ML server 
Then she followed up with “what if the ML server failed to add the recipe?”, 
to which I replied “I’d store a sort of flag variable, which detects if there is 
any error code returned from the ML server. If the backend server 
successfully added the data, I’d send a delete request to it.” Then she asked 
something along the lines of “how would you adapt this if the backend and 
ML are also connected” (don’t remember exactly what it was) So then I 
mentioned that my frontend would make one API call to the backend, and 
the backend would make one API call to the ML server. Then if the ML server 
fails, it will return the error code to the backend, which would just issue a 
database query, instead of the more expensive API call in the first solution. 
This was the last question on my project, and after this she moved on to the 
DSA portion of the interview. 
 
DSA Question 
Given an array of integers nums and an integer target k, find one continuous 
subarray whose elements sum up to k. Return the start and end indices 
(inclusive) of any such subarray. 
Example: arr = [5,2,3,4,1,2,3], Target = 10. Then l = 1, r = 4 was expected.

Python
 
I did not get the entire question at once, rather she started with an array and 
a required target, and highlighted a certain subarray that would sum to this 
target. Initially I thought I was being asked the “two sum” problem (would 
have been crazy), because the first subarray was just of length 2. But then 
she mentioned another target to which the answer was a longer subarray. 
I clarified exactly what she required, and started solving. 
Initially I proposed the brute force solution of checking all subarrays, which 
would take O(n^2) time. Then I moved on to the optimal solution by 
proposing use of prefix arrays (she had also built on to the question by use 
of prefix arrays only). I was a bit skeptical about my solution as I had only 
solved the variation where we get the count of subarrays, not exact indices. 
But in the end I provided the correct solution, with a short dry run and 
python code (code was not required).  
I also thought of providing a sliding window approach, but time ran out and 
that would not have worked for negative numbers anyways. 
 
def subarraySumOneIndices(nums, k): 
    prefix_map = {0: -1} 
    prefix_sum = 0 
 
    for i, num in enumerate(nums): 
        prefix_sum += num 
        if prefix_sum - k in prefix_map: 
            return (prefix_map[prefix_sum - k] + 1, i) 
        prefix_map[prefix_sum] = i 
 
    return None 
 
While writing the code I also mentioned python specific constructs, like how 
a hashmap is declared in python, how we can’t use the ‘map’ keyword as it is 
reserved etc. (not needed at all, they just wanted the approach and dry run)

After the DSA problem, she asked me if I had any questions for her. During 
their main introduction at 8 am she had mentioned that she works with Java 
and Spring Boot. So I brought that up and asked “what was the biggest 
challenge that you have faced?” to which she answered for about 2-3 
minutes.  
 
I came out of round 1 at 9-9:10 am a bit anxious and unsure because I felt I 
had not communicated the DSA solution properly. But, sometime later, I was 
informed that my round 2 would be conducted in a while.

Round 2 - Design Round 
10:45 am  
Duration: 40-45 mins  
 
The interviewer for the design round was asking everyone their hobbies, and 
then asking to implement an application related to a particular hobby.  
 
This design round wasn't strictly related to traditional LLD/HLD, but it was 
just a round to see how I would approach designing any application, no real 
technical terms were expected. 
 
I was asked to design an app which would let an individual learn an 
instrument. 
 
He started by asking what I would add as features in my application. I said 
that first we should create a registration platform, where the user can 
choose his previous experience with instruments & music in general. Then 
the user should be able to start with learning the basics of the instrument 
i.e. how to play notes, chords etc. The user should also be able to learn 
particular songs of their choice. I focused on keyboard and guitar as example 
cases for this application. For the guitar I also mentioned that the app could 
provide a tuner to tune the strings, but the interviewer said that it's fine if 
we don't implement that as of now. 
 
After this, he asked me to design the high level architecture along with 
information on what data I would store in the application. I started by saying 
that someone who wants to learn an instrument would probably find a 
mobile app ideal due to portability, so we should make a mobile app for the 
front-end. For the data, I spoke about storing chords, scales, notes and how 
to play these on different instruments. I also spoke about storing individual

songs and the ways to play these on different instruments; I mentioned that 
we could utilise Inheritance if there is any common factor between ways to 
play a song/scale by an instrument; for example, a song/scale that just 
consists of a sequence of notes would play the same on any instrument, only 
the way to play those particular notes would differ. 
He asked me how songs are stored on streaming services such as Spotify and 
Amazon music, to which I replied they directly store .mp3 files as large 
objects. I was also asked how exactly I would store the songs, to which I 
provided two options: 
-​ A large object (such as a pdf file) of the sheet music of the song 
-​ A string consisting of the sequence of notes 
I think the interviewer also had experience with instruments so I could easily 
communicate my points across to him. 
 
After all this, he asked me how I would implement certain features. 
 
Feature 1: The app should be able to detect what note is being played. 
I said that the phone should be able to detect the frequency of the note 
being played. But maybe the frequency detected isn’t exactly the frequency 
that is stored in our database (or in memory), so I suggested that we could 
store frequencies in a sorted array, and whenever a note is played we just 
return the upper/lower bound frequency (whichever is closer) to the current 
frequency using binary search. I don’t remember in what context I said this 
but I also suggested that we could store note->frequency mapping in a 
relational database and use an SQL query to return the upper/lower bound.  
 
Feature 2: The app should be able to detect what song is being played based 
on some notes. 
I talked about using an ML model (as a form of brute force) but I had a 
feeling that he wasn't looking for that, I also highlighted some drawbacks of

using it (such as training the model on different parts of a song individually). 
After this, I gave two approaches, for which I assumed that the song is being 
stored as a string of notes. 
 
1) Sliding Window 
Now before all this, I mentioned that we shouldn’t expect our app to detect 
songs if only 1-2 notes are played and that a sequence of sufficient length 
should be played. Given this sequence, we could use a sliding window 
algorithm to detect if that sequence is part of any song. This would be easy 
to implement as our input sequence would be of fixed length only. But the 
drawback here is that every song would have to be searched. 
 
2) Trie 
My explanation wasn’t complete here, I just mentioned that we could store 
all the song sequences in a trie data structure. I drew out an example 
structure and showed how searching could be done. I also highlighted that 
the Trie method could not be used for detecting sequences in the middle of 
songs, only for the starting parts, and ended it there.  
 
I also thought about mentioning string hashing, but I wasn’t really familiar 
with it and time ran out anyways. In the end, my interviewer asked me if I 
had any questions for him. He had not mentioned his role at the firm so I 
asked him about it, to which he answered sufficiently. 
 
 
The round ended at 11:30 am, after which they told me to come back at 
1pm. I used the remaining time to talk to my fellow candidates and to have 
lunch. But due to more interviews being conducted, they only announced 
the shortlists for round 3 at 2:45pm, and said that round 3 will start from 
3:15 onwards.

Round 3 - DSA + Resume 
3:25pm 
Duration: 10-15 mins 
 
After eliminations from the first two rounds, 9 people made it to the third 
round. Some of us had a technical round while others had an HR round. One 
of us did not have his round 3 conducted at all, maybe due to time 
constraints.  
 
I'll keep this one short, just like the interview itself. 
 
1)​I walked in, greeted my interviewer, gave my intro, and the interviewer 
gave his intro and talked about what he does at the company. 
2)​The interviewer asked me if I’ve used AI tools (yes), if I’ve used testing 
tools (no), and asked me to explain the features of one of my projects 
and the AI feature of my project in depth. 
3)​He then proceeded to ask me a DSA question - Next Greater Element. I 
just had to provide an overview of the general working of the 
algorithm - once I mentioned the term “monotonic stack” and 
explained how the stack is being used, he was satisfied with my 
answer. 
 
This concluded my round 3. 
 
Results 
At 5pm, results were announced and 6 of us were selected, including me.

Final thoughts on the interview 
I felt that the interview was easier than expected. As I had read interview 
experiences, I prepared more topics outside of array questions such as 
Binary Search, Trees, Linked Lists etc. so I was surprised that only array based 
questions were asked. The monotonic stack question was still unexpected, 
but I had prepared that too. I was also not asked CS fundamentals (they did 
not ask last year too) and HR questions (but in any case always prepare for 
these). The design question was expected due to similar reasons but 
everyone was asked a different question, based on their hobbies. Also the 
team had a flight to catch, so they wanted to be done with it as fast as 
possible.  
 
This concludes my interview experience.

General Preparation Tips 
1. For core DSA concepts, solve any DSA sheet. I’d recommend the Striver 
A2Z sheet. Avoid solving problems randomly. Instead, progress step by step 
through the sheet to build concepts systematically. Solve daily problems 
from LeetCode and GFG to build a routine. 
2. Review core Computer Science fundamentals, including Operating 
Systems(OS), Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS), and Database 
Management Systems (DBMS). If time allows, explore Computer Networks 
and low/high-level design concepts. Companies like DE Shaw ask LLD/HLD 
questions (read Rushabh Mehta’s experience).  
3. Focus on key interview questions related to your preferred programming 
language. Apart from this you should be familiar with at least one of Java 
and C++, as companies tend to ask language specific questions and OOP 
questions from these languages. 
4. Know your resume inside out. Be ready to answer questions about the 
technologies used in your projects. 
5. Prepare for HR questions too, use the STAR method to answer questions. 
 
OA Tips 
1. Take part in CP contests to sharpen your problem-solving speed. For OA’s 
I'd recommend pure CP based contests like on CodeChef and CodeForces 
(first few questions of contests), as many OA questions are based on pure 
logic and not on any core DSA concept. Some companies tend to ask 
extremely hard OA questions, so I’d recommend trying later questions also, 
and to at least have some knowledge about advanced data structures used 
in competitive programming. For example, the 2nd question of the HILTI OA 
was based on advanced data structures for many candidates, and the BNY 
OA was like a CF contest only (read Siddhesh Pandey’s experience for BNY).   
2. Use a language you are comfortable with (preferably the same language 
used for contests) and have a good grasp on the syntax and inbuilt libraries

and data structures for a particular language. Examples would include STL 
for C++, collections for python and java etc. You should mainly know how to 
sort, how to use arrays/vectors (depending on your language), HashMaps 
and HashSets. 
3. Read the complexity guide on codeforces, to know what time complexity 
is expected based on constraints on data. This helps in OAs, contests and 
problem solving in general.  
 
Interview Tips 
1. Before going into the interview, research about the company, their goals, 
their values etc. A good source for this is the Pre Placement Talk conducted 
by the company, so always pay attention to that. You can also research on 
the Company’s website. You can incorporate this knowledge into your HR 
question responses, or ask them questions about it if they allow (usually 
most interviews ask if we have any questions for them - this is a good chance 
to show your genuine interest in the company.) 
2. During interviews, it’s essential to communicate your thought process 
clearly. Speaking out loud while solving problems not only helps interviewers 
follow your logic but also gives them the opportunity to provide hints if 
you're heading in the wrong direction. It’s equally important to mention 
edge cases , as it shows your thorough approach to tackling challenges. But 
always start basic and then work on edge cases. For open ended questions 
such as design questions, always follow up with the interviewer about 
requirements.  
3. Do some mock interviews with peers or seniors, ask them for feedback on 
your performance, and use it to improve yourself.
